scenes.heading: First Nations knowledge of adaptations
scenes.sub: Knowledge of Country, built over many generations
scenes.say: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have cared for Australia's lands and waters for tens of thousands of years. Their detailed knowledge of plants, animals, seasons and fire connects closely with adaptation and interdependence.

scenes.heading: Respecting the knowledge
points: Many distinct groups, each with its own Country
Country: lands, waters, skies, all living things
scenes.say: There are many distinct First Nations groups, each with its own Country: the lands, waters, skies and living things it is connected to and cares for. So there's no single body of knowledge. It's living knowledge that belongs to its communities. Use it with permission, and credit the knowledge holders.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Jacarandas flower around exam time each year
scenes.science: A biological indicator: one event signals another
scenes.breaks: Jacarandas and exams line up by coincidence. A true indicator reflects real ecological links, observed on Country over generations.
scenes.say: Here's an everyday comparison for the biology idea. In many cities, jacarandas flower around exam time. That's phenology: the timing of a seasonal event. A biological indicator goes deeper. A tree flowering can signal a fish breeding run, because both respond to the same changes in the environment.

scenes.heading: Seasonal calendars
points: Based on local changes, not fixed dates
Often more or fewer than four seasons
Guide when to harvest, and when to leave
scenes.say: Many groups use seasonal calendars based on local changes, not fixed dates, often with more or fewer than four seasons. Indicators guide when to harvest, and when to leave resources alone to recover. That reflects interdependence and sustainability.

scenes.heading: Cultural burning
scenes.say: Cultural burning is the use of fire by First Nations peoples to care for Country. Fires are cool and low-intensity, burnt in patches to make a mosaic, and timed by reading Country. It must be led by the communities who hold that knowledge.

scenes.heading: Comparing fire regimes
scenes.question: A hypothetical study: Area A has regular, patchy, cool burns. Area B is unburnt for years, then has an intense wildfire. Compare.
lines: A: less dry fuel, so fires stay cooler
A: most trees survive; animals shelter
B: hot fire kills trees, seeds and animals
Answer: cool, patchy burns protect habitat
scenes.say: In a hypothetical study, Area A has regular, patchy, cool burns. Area B goes unburnt for years, then has an intense wildfire. Area A has less dry fuel, so fires stay cooler and most trees survive. In Area B, the hot fire is more likely to kill trees, seeds and animals.

scenes.heading: Two ways of knowing

left.title: First Nations knowledge
points: Links people, land and living things

scenes.say: These are two knowledge systems, both built on careful observation. First Nations knowledge is often holistic, linking people, land and living things. Western science often tests one variable at a time. Together, in two-way learning, they give a fuller picture of ecosystems.

points: Many nations, many Countries, many calendars
scenes.say: Quick recap. Each nation holds knowledge of its own Country. Seasonal calendars use indicators that show phenology and interdependence. Cultural burning is cool, patchy and timed by reading Country. And always respect the knowledge holders. Now try the practice questions!
